bib.title: What is a machine learning engineer? (Chapter 1, Machine Learning Engineering in Action)

question: What does an ML engineer do, and which project practices prevent the common reasons applied ML projects fail?
contributions: Six-phase ML engineering road map (planning, scoping and research, experimentation, development, deployment, evaluation)
Author's estimate of six causes of ML project failure

results.claim: Planning failures are the largest cause of ML project failure in the author's estimate.
results.metric: share of ML project failures attributed to planning
results.setup: Author's own rough estimate from experience (hundreds of projects worked on or advised), not a measured sample; Fig 1.2

results.claim: Scoping problems are the second largest cause.
results.setup: Author's own rough estimate from experience (hundreds of projects worked on or advised), not a measured sample; Fig 1.2

results.claim: Technology and fragility each account for 15% of failures.
results.setup: Author's own rough estimate from experience (hundreds of projects worked on or advised), not a measured sample; Fig 1.2

results.claim: Cost accounts for 10% of failures and hubris for 5%.
results.setup: Author's own rough estimate from experience (hundreds of projects worked on or advised), not a measured sample; Fig 1.2

results.claim: Failures are mostly inexperience or miscommunication with the business, never malice.
results.quote: Generally, these failures happen because the DS team is either inexperienced with solving a problem of the scale required (a technological or process-driven failure) or hasn’t fully understood the desired outcome from the business (a communication-driven failure).

results.claim: Planning should fix what and why, not how or when; the email-timing example was solved by an analytics query on time zones, not a recommender.
results.setup: Hypothetical marketing email open-rate scenario; illustrative story
results.quote: By focusing on what will be built and why it needs to be built, both the DS team and the business are able to guide the discussion more fruitfully.

results.claim: Scoping: a junior team (blog search, XGBoost, two weeks) and a research team (implement a paper from scratch, months, multi-GPU) both fail; take a middle path.
results.setup: Hypothetical fraud-detection scoping scenario, Figs 1.5 and 1.6; illustrative, not data
results.quote: Team A would likely estimate about two weeks to build its XGBoost binary classification model

results.claim: Experimentation is a Goldilocks activity: too few options hides flaws (cherry-picked samples, two product classes), too many causes analysis paralysis and budget burn.
results.setup: Hypothetical shelf-product image classifier scenario, Figs 1.7 and 1.8; the author says he has seen the over-testing case many dozens of times
results.quote: Testing approaches is a Goldilocks activity; if you don’t test enough options, you’re probably not finding the best solution, while testing too many things wastes precious time.

results.claim: Modular, config-driven, tested code on Git feature branches avoids the merge conflicts of a monolithic notebook.
results.setup: Hypothetical two-data-scientist feature-engineering change, Figs 1.9 and 1.10
results.quote: With a fully modularized code base registered in Git, each of them can check out a feature branch from the master, make small edits to the modules that are part of their features, write new tests (if needed), run their tests, and submit a pull request.

results.claim: Design deployment at project start: an underpowered stack cannot serve, an overpowered one burns money.
results.setup: Fast-food inventory scenario moving from weekly batch to near-real-time per-store ARIMA with Kafka, Spark Structured Streaming, MLflow, REST; illustrative
results.quote: If it’s underpowered, the prediction quality doesn’t matter (since the infrastructure can’t properly serve the predictions). If it’s overpowered, you’re effectively burning money on unused infrastructure and complexity.

results.claim: In the inventory story, cloud costs after week one exceeded the savings by more than an order of magnitude and the project was cancelled.
results.value: more than an order of magnitude
results.setup: Hypothetical story; author says he has personally caused this three times
results.quote: cloud computing costs are more than an order of magnitude higher than the cost savings

results.claim: Use the simplest architecture: batch for weekly cadence, a database and one VM for MB-scale data, CPUs when training takes minutes.
results.quote: If the project requires a periodicity of inference of one week, use a batch process (not real-time streaming). If the data volumes are in the megabytes, use a database and a simple virtual machine (not a 25-node Apache Spark cluster). If the runtime of training is measured in minutes, stick to CPUs (not GPUs).

results.claim: Deployment cost scales with SLA, drift volatility, training complexity and prediction volume; the costly extreme is online serving with SLA under 50 ms and retraining more often than hourly.
results.metric: example online-serving SLA at the costly extreme
results.setup: Qualitative cost-axis diagram, Fig 1.13; no costs measured
results.quote: Active retraining, online serving, SLA < 50 ms

results.claim: Without agreed attribution (A/B test, revenue lift with estimation error) a good production model can be cancelled when asked what it earns.
results.setup: Hypothetical; Fig 1.14 shows an invented $63,750 per quarter project cost; author says it took him two hard lessons
results.quote: The only thing that they can do to give attribution to their model is to perform A/B testing and use sound statistical models to arrive at a revenue lift calculation (with estimation errors) to show how much additional sales are due to their model.

results.claim: Summary: six phases (planning, scoping and research, experimentation, development, deployment, evaluation) reduce abandonment risk.
results.quote: Focusing on best practices throughout the six primary project phases of applied ML work—planning, scoping and research, experimentation, development, deployment, and evaluation—will greatly help a project minimize risk of abandonment.

limits: All numbers and scenarios are the author's experience or invented examples; no dataset, sample size or method for the Fig 1.2 failure shares.
The text describes itself as 'my biased view of working with only so many companies'.
Tooling remarks (Kafka, Spark, MLflow, ARIMA) are illustrative and dated; chapter 11 is cited for A/B testing but is not in this file.
The PDF does not print the author name or year.
practices: Hold a planning discussion on what and why, not how or when, with the business sponsor; ask how it is done now, how predictions will be used, what success is (Fig 1.4, 1.2.1).
Name subject-matter experts and get them involved early (Fig 1.4).
Scope with a research phase long enough to find hidden gotchas but avoid implementing cutting-edge papers from scratch; balance academic and applied views (1.2.2).
Keep experimentation bounded: a few candidate approaches, a phased MVP, and test on non-cherry-picked data (1.2.3, Fig 1.15).
Write modular, configuration-driven code with unit and integration tests and Git feature branches (1.2.4).
Pick the simplest architecture that meets the SLA, volume and drift needs: batch for weekly cadence, VM and database for MB data, CPUs when training takes minutes (1.2.5 sidebar).
Estimate total cost of ownership and cancel early in planning if the project is not worth it (1.2.5).
Agree attribution metrics during planning and plan an A/B test before full rollout (1.2.6).
Monitor cost, SLA, usage, drift, and retrain (Fig 1.15).

terms.definition: It uses a set of standards, tools, processes, and methodology that aims to minimize the chances of abandoned, misguided, or irrelevant work being done in an effort to solve a business problem or need.
